input.content:
Suppose a policy could deny reading the `auth` scope itself. A peer could then sync a document *without* its policy, see an uninitialized auth scope, and allow every operation it holds; replicas would diverge permanently. The `auth` and `document` scopes therefore **bypass the grants**: the policy and the document's metadata are visible to any holder of the document, and grants gate domain-scope reads only.

The same reasoning carries the rule into every read path. A read that narrows scopes has the `auth` scope added back before the fetch, because a model built without the policy reads as uninitialized; `initialState` is filtered alongside `state` since it holds the same scope names; and a replica denied a domain scope simply never receives that stream, so partial replication stays consistent — it never holds or evaluates what it may not read.

For consumers this means a `PHDocument` has four state scopes — `auth`, `document`, `global`, `local` — of which only `global` and `local` are gateable. The `scoped-reads` recipe uses exactly that pair: expenses in `global`, reviewers' confidential notes in `local` (conventionally node-local data, used here as the second gateable scope because there is no third). A scope the subject may not read comes back **absent from `document.state`**, not present and empty.

The exemption extends to group rosters: a replica must fold a group's membership to evaluate a policy that names it, so a named group's member list is served to that policy's audience regardless of the group's own read grants — bounded by the rules in the group-serving note.
